items.followUp: Differentiate between a coenzyme and a metal-ion cofactor.

rubric.why: Identifies the defining attachment of a prosthetic group.
rubric.description: A prosthetic group is firmly or tightly attached to its enzyme.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is firmly or tightly attached.

rubric.why: Distinguishes a coenzyme from a prosthetic group by its weaker attachment.
rubric.description: A coenzyme is loosely or temporarily attached to its enzyme.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is loosely or temporarily attached.

modelAnswer: A prosthetic group is a non-protein component that remains firmly attached to an enzyme.
A coenzyme is a non-protein organic component that is loosely attached to an enzyme.

items.followUp: Describe how an enzyme and its substrate interact according to the induced-fit model.

rubric.why: Explains the specific fit between the substrate and the enzyme’s active site.
rubric.description: The substrate fits the enzyme’s specifically shaped active site, like a key fitting a lock.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the specific fit between substrate and active site.

rubric.why: Includes the result of binding and the enzyme’s role after the reaction.
rubric.description: An enzyme-substrate complex forms; products are released and the enzyme remains unchanged.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the complex and release of products or the unchanged enzyme.

modelAnswer: The substrate has a shape that fits the enzyme’s active site, like a key fits a lock.
An enzyme-substrate complex forms; the reaction produces products, which leave the enzyme unchanged.

items.followUp: Differentiate between food in the oesophagus and food in the stomach after digestion begins.

rubric.why: Identifies the bolus and how it is formed.
rubric.description: A bolus is chewed food mixed with saliva.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the bolus as food mixed with saliva.

rubric.why: Identifies chyme and its formation in the stomach.
rubric.description: Chyme is the semi-liquid food mixed with gastric juice in the stomach.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing chyme as semi-liquid food mixed with gastric juice.

modelAnswer: A bolus is chewed food mixed with saliva in the mouth.
Chyme is semi-liquid, partially digested food mixed with gastric juice in the stomach.

items.followUp: What can happen if too little water is reabsorbed from the large intestine?

rubric.why: Recognises the condition described in the question.
rubric.description: Too much water is reabsorbed from the intestine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying excessive water reabsorption.

rubric.why: States the effect of excessive water removal from the intestinal contents.
rubric.description: The faeces become hard and dry, causing constipation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for constipation or hard, dry faeces.

modelAnswer: If excessive water is reabsorbed from the intestine, the faeces become hard and dry.
This may cause constipation.

items.followUp: Trace the path of blood through systemic circulation.

rubric.why: Identifies the starting point and destination for blood to be oxygenated.
rubric.description: Deoxygenated blood flows from the right ventricle to the lungs and becomes oxygenated.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the right ventricle-to-lungs route and oxygenation.

rubric.why: Completes the return route of pulmonary circulation.
rubric.description: Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs to the left atrium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the return of oxygenated blood to the left atrium.

modelAnswer: Pulmonary circulation is the flow of blood from the right ventricle to the lungs for oxygenation.
Oxygenated blood then returns from the lungs to the left atrium.

items.followUp: Define biology and name its three major divisions, explaining what each studies.

rubric.why: Gives the meaning of biology.
rubric.description: Biology is the study of life or living organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition of biology.

rubric.why: Identifies the division concerned with plants.
rubric.description: Botany is the study of plants.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for botany and plants.

rubric.why: Identifies the division concerned with animals.
rubric.description: Zoology is the study of animals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for zoology and animals.

rubric.why: Identifies the division concerned with microorganisms and completes the list of major divisions.
rubric.description: Microbiology is the study of microorganisms.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for naming microbiology and stating that it studies microorganisms.

modelAnswer: Biology is the study of life or living organisms.
Botany is the study of plants.
Zoology is the study of animals.
Microbiology is the study of microorganisms.

items.followUp: Compare arteries, veins and capillaries in terms of their walls and the direction or role of blood flow.

rubric.why: Describes the artery’s structure and direction of blood flow.
rubric.description: Arteries have thick, elastic walls and carry blood away from the heart.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the thick wall and flow away from the heart.

rubric.why: Distinguishes veins by their walls, valves or direction of flow.
rubric.description: Veins have thinner walls, often contain valves, and carry blood towards the heart.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct vein feature and its direction of flow.

rubric.why: States the characteristic structure of capillary walls.
rubric.description: Capillary walls are only one cell thick.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the one-cell-thick capillary wall.

rubric.why: Explains the capillary’s role in exchange between blood and tissues.
rubric.description: Capillaries allow exchange of materials between blood and body tissues.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing exchange as the capillary function.

modelAnswer: Arteries have thick, elastic walls and carry blood away from the heart.
Veins have thinner walls, contain valves, and carry blood towards the heart.
Capillaries have walls only one cell thick.
This thin wall allows exchange of materials between the blood and body tissues.

items.followUp: Define an endangered species and give examples found in Pakistan, with reasons their numbers may decline.

rubric.why: Defines endangered species in terms of its risk of extinction.
rubric.description: An endangered species is one at risk of extinction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition referring to the risk of extinction.

rubric.why: Provides examples of endangered animals found in Pakistan.
rubric.description: Examples include the Indus dolphin, snow leopard, Marco Polo sheep, green sea turtle and houbara bustard.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for two correct examples, 1 mark for each.

rubric.why: Identifies a human cause of declining populations.
rubric.description: Hunting or poaching reduces their numbers.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming hunting, poaching or overhunting.

rubric.why: Identifies another major cause of declining populations.
rubric.description: Habitat destruction or loss threatens their survival.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming habitat destruction or loss.

modelAnswer: An endangered species is a species whose population has fallen so much that it is at risk of extinction.
Examples of endangered animals in Pakistan include the Indus dolphin and the snow leopard.
Other examples include the Marco Polo sheep, green sea turtle and houbara bustard.
Hunting and poaching reduce the numbers of these animals.
Habitat destruction or loss also threatens their survival.
